cases.abstract: FlexGen enables throughput-oriented large language model inference when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. It formulates offloading as graph traversal and uses a cost model and linear programming to place tensors across GPU, CPU, and disk. Block scheduling reuses loaded weights across GPU batches, while cache offloading permits larger batches. An idealized analysis without CPU computation bounds asymptotic weight I/O within twice the optimum. Four-bit compression of weights and caches reduces storage and transfers without retraining or calibration. In dummy-weight benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32 generated tokens, OPT-175B on one 16-GB T4 with 208-GB CPU memory and a 1.5-TB SSD achieves 0.69 tokens/s without compression and 1.12 tokens/s with compression, versus 0.01 tokens/s for both uncompressed Accelerate and DeepSpeed. Separate real-weight evaluations show small Lambada accuracy and WikiText perplexity changes, including with sparse value-cache access, although compression can reduce throughput for models fitting GPU memory. Across four GPUs, offloaded models show super-linear decoding scaling but sublinear overall scaling when generating 32 tokens. FlexGen completes seven HELM sub-scenarios with OPT-IML-30B in 21 hours, including system overhead. The demonstrated gains serve batch workloads accepting long completion times and depend on host-memory capacity and storage bandwidth.
cases.notes: Central contribution: throughput-oriented offloading through weight reuse and cache placement, supported by Sections 4 and 6.1 and Tables 2/15. Compression is a co-contribution, evaluated with real weights in Table 5; throughput benchmarks use dummy weights. The factor-two bound concerns idealized asymptotic weight I/O, not runtime optimality. The abstract retains compression slowdowns and the distinction between decoding and overall scaling. HELM supplies an end-to-end use case. Petals comparisons are omitted because they normalize different GPU counts.

cases.abstract: We introduce neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) models that parameterize continuous hidden-state dynamics with a neural network and use a numerical solver to compute outputs. Adjoint sensitivities train these models through a reverse-time augmented ODE without storing intermediate solver operations, giving memory cost independent of the number of function evaluations. Solver tolerances control the precision-computation trade-off. On MNIST, an ODE network achieves 0.42% test error with 0.22 million parameters, versus 0.41% and 0.60 million for a residual network. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem expresses log-density evolution through a Jacobian trace rather than a determinant. This enables continuous normalizing flows with additive hidden units and linear density-update cost per function evaluation; two-dimensional experiments illustrate density matching and reversible sampling. A latent ODE model represents irregularly observed time series through shared continuous dynamics and can jointly model observation times using a Poisson likelihood. On synthetic noisy spirals using 30 of 100 observations, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN on 100 prediction times extending beyond training observations. Reverse-time trajectory reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing can mitigate it by storing intermediate states.
cases.notes: Central contribution: trainable continuous dynamics, not superior classification. Section 2 and Table 1 support the memory and parameter argument; Theorem 1 establishes the separate density-modeling contribution under stated regularity conditions. Table 2 supports prediction beyond training observations only on synthetic spirals. Flow comparisons use different optimizers and iteration budgets, so matched-budget superiority is not claimed. Constant memory refers to solver evaluations, not parameter count; checkpointing changes that trade-off. Garbled software names and tolerance values are omitted.
